title: Every CEO Job Is a First CEO Job
author: Managing the Future
summary: The author argues that the CEO role is fundamentally non-portable in a way that distinguishes it from every other executive function: CFOs, CMOs, and CHROs carry a mental model that translates from company to company, but CEOs are integrators whose value-creation task resets with each new organizational ecosystem. Two reasons explain the non-portability: most CEOs lack an explicit model for the role (making each new position feel like relearning business basics), and even with a framework like CEO-S, the integration task -- balancing shareholders, customers, and employees -- looks radically different at a PE-backed industrial company versus a venture-funded SaaS business. The practical response the article recommends is twofold: develop an explicit mental model for how the CEO role creates value, and become an aggressive fast learner by compressing the normal learning cycle well below its default rhythms. Specific compression tactics include skip-level meetings (which give a less polished picture of how things actually work than direct reports can provide), weekly customer conversations for the first three months, and biweekly coaching rather than monthly. The author characterizes the CEOs who succeed in unfamiliar situations as those who get interested rather than defensive when a metric looks off -- treating the new role as a puzzle to be solved rather than a territory to defend.
points: Functional executive expertise (CFO, CMO, etc.) is portable because the core value-creation model transfers across companies; CEO expertise is not, because the integrator role -- balancing shareholders, customers, and employees -- resets uniquely in each organizational ecosystem.

CEOs without an explicit model for the role re-learn the basics of business every time they start a new position; developing a structured framework for how the CEO role creates value is the only way to translate the portable 10% of the job.

The fastest path to learning a new CEO role is to compress feedback cycles below their default rhythms: skip-level meetings, weekly customer conversations for three months, and biweekly coaching instead of monthly, to get more learning reps in the first 90 days.

Skip-level meetings are particularly useful because the layer below direct reports carries a less polished, less managed picture of how things actually work -- the raw organizational reality that direct reports have learned to package.

CEOs who succeed in unfamiliar situations share a particular orientation: they get interested rather than defensive when metrics look off, treating the new role as a puzzle to understand before they try to fix it.
quotes: When an experienced CFO takes a new job, they bring their entire playbook with them... Most executive roles are similar in that regard. CEOs don't have that luxury. Every time they step into a new role, they are essentially starting over.

Functional expertise is portable. CEOs are integrators of the functional areas and balancers of the interests of shareholders, customers, and employees. That balance is going to look very different at a PE-backed industrial company at $200M in revenue than it will at a venture-funded SaaS business at the same size.
Start as the humble student. Don't over-rely on old patterns that served you in the previous context. Talk to people at the new company and really listen, with both ears and an open mind.

Many of the CEO's tools for learning operate on longer cycles (monthly peer group, quarterly board meeting, annual customer conference, etc.). Those rhythms aren't fast enough on their own. Compress the cycle by adding higher-frequency inputs.
Skip-level meetings are particularly useful here, because the layer below your direct reports usually has a less polished view of how things actually work.

The CEOs I have watched succeed in unfamiliar situations tend to share a particular orientation toward not knowing things. They get interested rather than defensive. When a metric looks off, they want to understand why before they want to fix it.
Every CEO job is a first CEO job. This is why it's a role that has always rewarded the fastest learners.
